prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Other weddings are so shrewd on the sofa, short and baffled, bassett-legged. All things knuckled, I have no winter left, in my sore rememory, to melt down for drinking water. Shrunk down. Your wedding slides the way wiry dark hairs do, down a swimming pool drain. So I am drained. Sincerely. I wish you every chapped bird on this pilgrimage to hold your hem up from the dust. Dust is plural: infinite dust. I will sink in the sun, I will crawl towards the heavy drawing and design the curtains in the room of never marrying you. Because it is a sinking, because today’s perfect weather is a later life’s smut. This soiled future unplans love. I keep unplanning the same Sunday. Leg and flower, breeze and terrier, I have no garden and couldn’t be happier. Please, don’t lose me here. I am sorry my clutch is all tendon and no discipline: the heart is a severed kind of muscle and alone. I can hear yours in your room. I hear mine in another room. In another’s.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Other, All, Shrunk

outputs.L1:
Other weddings are so shrewd on the sofa—short, baffled, basset-legged. All things knuckled, I have no winter left in my sore rememory to melt down for drinking water. Shrunk down. Your wedding slides the way wiry dark hairs do—down a swimming pool drain. And so I am drained. Sincerely.

I wish you every chapped bird on this pilgrimage to hold your hem above the dust. Dust is plural: infinite dust. I will sink in the sun. I will crawl toward the heavy drawing and design the curtains in the room of never marrying you. Because it is a sinking; because today’s perfect weather is a later life’s smut. This soiled future unplans love. I keep unplanning the same Sunday.

Leg and flower, breeze and terrier: I have no garden and couldn’t be happier. Please, don’t lose me here. I am sorry my clutch is all tendon and no discipline. The heart is a severed kind of muscle, and alone. I can hear yours in your room. I hear mine in another room. In another’s.
outputs.L2:
Those other marriages sit cleverly on the couch—stunted, bewildered, with the squat limbs of a basset hound. Everything bends at the joints. In the ache of my remembered past, no winter remains for me to thaw into water. Everything has withered. Your marriage slips away like coarse black strands spiraling through a pool’s drain, leaving me emptied. Truly. May every bird with cracked skin along this journey lift your clothing clear of the dirt. And dirt is never singular; it is endless.

I will descend beneath the sunlight. I will inch toward the weighty sketch and draft drapes for the chamber where I never become your spouse. It is a descent, after all, and the flawless sky of this day will become the grime of some future existence. That stained tomorrow dismantles love before it can happen. Again and again, I undo the plans for one particular Sunday. Limb beside blossom, wind beside small dog: I own no patch of earth, and my joy could not be greater.

Please do not let me disappear in this place. Forgive the way I grasp—with sinew but without restraint. A heart is merely isolated muscle, cut loose. From here, I can make out yours beating where you are. My own pulse reaches me from elsewhere—from a room belonging to someone else.
outputs.L3:
The speaker experiences the beloved’s wedding to someone else as a profound emotional loss. Rather than sharing in the celebration, they feel drained and diminished, as though the marriage has taken something essential from them. Yet their grief does not turn into bitterness. Despite the pain, the speaker sincerely wishes the couple protection, grace, and safety as they begin their shared journey.

At the same time, the speaker imagines a future shaped by permanent separation: they will never marry the person they love. They repeatedly attempt to resist, erase, or undo that love, but their efforts only reveal how deeply attached they remain. Images of dust, sinking, and soiling darken the wedding’s apparent happiness, suggesting that joy is fragile and may eventually decay into regret, disappointment, or sorrow.

The emotional distance between the speaker and the beloved is captured most painfully through the image of two hearts separated by a room. The speaker can still sense the beloved’s presence, but can no longer reach them. Their own lonely heart continues to respond from afar, emphasizing both the persistence of their love and the finality of their exclusion from the beloved’s new life.
outputs.L4:
The speaker responds to another person’s wedding with a mixture of grief, disbelief, and estrangement. Instead of describing the loss directly, they filter it through surreal domestic and natural imagery: dust gathers, drains carry things away, weather presses against the body, and separate rooms become symbols of emotional distance. The wedding, ordinarily associated with union and renewal, is experienced as proof that a shared possibility has ended. Everything in the speaker’s surroundings seems altered by that knowledge, as though the external world has absorbed the shock.

Their repeated desire to “unplan” love suggests an impossible effort to reverse both memory and expectation. The speaker wants to dismantle not only the relationship but also the future once imagined around it—to undo the habits, hopes, and bodily attachments that continue after separation. Yet love cannot be canceled like an arrangement. It remains physical and involuntary, lodged in the heart and reflected in the speaker’s distorted perception of ordinary things.

The image of separate rooms captures the central tragedy: both people may still possess vulnerable, feeling hearts, but those hearts now exist in isolation. Emotional connection survives without the shared life that might have given it meaning. As a result, the imagined future is not simply abandoned; it is permanently marked by loss. The wedding confirms that time has moved forward, but the speaker remains caught between attachment and erasure, trying to undo a love that the body refuses to forget.
outputs.L5:
**The Other Side**

All the noise had faded, and the once-vast world had Shrunk to a single quiet room. On the Other side of the window, dawn appeared, bringing with it the promise that even the smallest life could begin again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem from the perspective of someone addressing the person they love on that person’s wedding day to someone else. Make it bitter, tender, fragmented, and full of strange domestic imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
Today you marry someone else, and the spoons know it.

They lie face-down in their drawer, little drowned saints. The kettle refuses to sing. Even the refrigerator, faithful white animal, has swallowed its own humming.

You are standing somewhere beneath flowers trained to behave.

I imagine your hands: those two pale rooms where I once misplaced my sleep. Someone is sliding a ring onto one of them now. A small gold lock. A bright, polite shackle. Everyone claps as if the house has not caught fire.

Beloved—

No. That word has crumbs in it. That word still wears your shirt to the sink at midnight.

I hope the cake is beautiful. I hope it tastes faintly of plaster and weather. I hope when you cut it, a flock of tiny moths escapes and settles in your new spouse’s hair like blessings nobody ordered.

Forgive me. I am trying to be tender.

May your towels always dry. May the pipes never speak my name. May you never open a cupboard and find the blue cup we broke, whole again, waiting.

You once said we would grow old badly together. We would become two bent forks arguing in the silverware tray. We would leave the stove on. We would feed the windows. We would forget every anniversary except the one when the ceiling leaked and we slept beneath an umbrella, laughing into each other’s wet mouths.

Instead, today.

Instead, bells.

Instead, your happiness buttoned up in someone else’s good coat.

I have placed my bitterness in the freezer beside the peas. By winter it will be a small green planet. By spring, perhaps, only ice. Do not worry about me. I have learned to set the table for ghosts: one plate, one knife, one chair pulled out for the absence that arrives precisely at seven.

When they ask if anyone objects, the oven light flickers three streets away.

That is all.

That is not all.

I love you with the uselessness of a hallway. I love you as dust loves the underside of the bed: secretly, completely, without improving anything.

Go now. Lift your veil, your glass, your new life.

I will be here, teaching the laundry how to mourn—  
your socks appearing among mine,  
impossible and warm,  
each one a soft mouth  
I cannot make stop saying  
yes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental epistolary poem about heartbreak, memory, and “unplanning” a shared future. Use images of dust, drains, gardens, curtains, weather, and separate rooms.
counterfactuals.output:
**Letters Toward an Unfuture**

**I. Dear You,**

Today I began unplanning the garden.

I lifted the names from the soil—  
lavender, thyme, the small blue flowers  
you said would return by themselves—  
and shook the future from their roots.

Dust rose like a second weather.

I am sorry for the tomatoes  
we will not argue over,  
for the green chairs fading patiently  
beneath a summer that no longer needs us.

Please disregard my previous letter  
regarding permanence.

It was written in rain.


**II. Dear House,**

Divide yourself.

Give me the room with the west window,  
give them the room where the pipes complain.  
Between us, hang curtains  
thin enough for light,  
thick enough for mercy.

At night the drains practice forgetting:  
water enters, circles once,  
then consents to disappearance.

Teach me that.


**III. Dear Memory,**

Your forwarding address is incorrect.

You keep sending:

—two cups beside the sink  
—mud drying on our shoes  
—the forecast pinned beneath a magnet  
—your hand opening the curtains  
as if morning were something we owned

Return to sender.

Return to that year.

Return, if possible,  
to dust.


**IV. Dear You, Again,**

I have canceled the October train,  
the yellow kitchen,  
the dog with the hypothetical name.

I have crossed out *we*  
wherever it appeared in the margins.

Still, weather arrives for both of us.

Somewhere you stand at another window,  
counting the seconds between lightning  
and its explanation.

Here, thunder enters my separate room  
without knocking.

I almost write:  
Are you afraid?

Instead, I close the curtain  
one inch at a time.


**V. Dear Future,**

Enclosed please find the following:

one key  
one packet of seeds  
one apology, unopened  
a floor plan torn down the middle

I do not know which half is mine.

Perhaps neither.

Perhaps a life is not a house  
but the dust that proves  
someone moved through it—  
touching shelves,  
leaving circles where the glasses stood,  
carrying what they could  
from room to room.


**VI. Postscript**

The garden, despite revisions,  
has begun.

Rain gathers in the gutters.  
Roots translate the dark.  
The drains keep swallowing  
every version of our names.

In separate rooms,  
under separate weather,  
we pull back separate curtains.

Morning does not ask  
what we had planned.

It enters anyway.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical paragraph beginning with “Other weddings are…” in which the speaker sincerely wishes an ex well while privately unraveling over their marriage. Include invented words and unsettling metaphors.
counterfactuals.output: Other weddings are bells and buttercream, but yours arrives like a small white animal gnawing through the walls of me. I hope the morning lays its gold hands gently on you both; I hope your vows grow roots, deep and weatherproof, and every room you share becomes warm with ordinary miracles. Truly, I wish you joy—even as my heart goes thinsilver and unbuttons itself, even as the old photographs begin whisperrotating in their drawer. Somewhere inside me, a brideshade lifts its veil and shows a mouth full of moths. I will raise my glass, I will smile, I will mean every blessing, while beneath my ribs the dark is quietly wedding itself to the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary prose poem about not marrying someone you once expected to marry. The voice should be intimate and grief-stricken, with surreal juxtapositions, bodily imagery, repetition, and ambiguous syntax.
counterfactuals.output:
**After the Future**

I did not marry you. The sentence keeps happening, a glass dropped in another room. I hear it at breakfast, among the blue spoons, while the refrigerator hums its small white weather. I did not marry you, and still my body arrives at the church of your body late, carrying flowers already brown at the edges. My hands remember a house we never entered. My mouth remembers the names of children we did not make, their bright shoes lined up in the dark.

Once, we spoke of forever as if it were a town just past the highway, as if we could miss the exit and circle back. There would be a yellow kitchen. There would be rain against the windows and your shirt on the chair and my hair in the drain, ordinary evidence, tender debris. Instead, I have this key with no door, this ring of pale skin where nothing was ever worn. Instead, Tuesday opens its metal throat. Instead, your absence sleeps beside me, warm as an animal, breathing with my lungs.

I did not marry you. You did not marry me. Somewhere, perhaps, the wedding continues without us: the cake cutting itself, the guests slow-dancing beneath a ceiling of moths. My mother is crying into a veil made of seawater. Your father raises a glass filled with small bones. We are there, we are not there, our almost-bodies turning toward each other when the music—when the music—

Sometimes I wake with my jaw aching from holding your name all night. Sometimes the heart is not a heart but a fist-sized room where two people keep missing each other by one second. I live there. You live there. No, neither of us lives there. The room goes on setting the table, folding the napkins, lighting one candle, then another, then another, for the marriage that did not happen, for the life that did, for whatever we were when we believed wanting was a kind of vow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a strange, emotionally raw wedding benediction from an abandoned lover. Avoid rhyme and conventional narrative; blend affectionate blessings with resentment, self-erasure, and images of animals, muscles, sunlight, and a future that has been soiled.
counterfactuals.output:
May the animal of your marriage sleep between you without biting.

May you wake beneath its warm ribs and call the pressure tenderness. May your hands, those small obedient muscles, learn each other’s weather until every gesture becomes instinct: the cup offered, the shoulder touched in passing, the door held open against winter.

I bless you with sunlight, though I resent how it enters every room without asking. Let it find you half-dressed, laughing, unashamed. Let it gild the bed where I am not. Let it expose nothing you cannot forgive.

I remove my name from your mouth. I take my coat from the hook of your future. I scrape my face from the photographs that have not yet been taken. See how generous I can be when there is no other shape left for me.

May your years together be strong as the tendon in a running deer, and just as frightened. May you know when to hold, when to release, when the body beside you is not a possession but a creature drinking in the dark.

I will not say I hope you are happy. Happiness is too clean a word for what you have done with tomorrow. You dragged it through mud. You let it roll among the dogs. You handed it back to me soiled with footprints and called that mercy.

Still: may the house stand. May illness pass over it. May grief, when it comes, sit quietly at your table and eat only what it needs. May neither of you become invisible to the other.

And if, years from now, sunlight touches the muscle of your beloved’s back and you feel the old terror of losing what you chose, remember that somewhere I survived becoming no one.

That is my gift.

That is my blessing.

Take it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
